# Phases of the Moon and Eclipses

Predict first. Why does the Moon change shape over a month? Earth's shadow?
Clouds? Its distance changing? Something about angles? Write down your
answer before you read on. About half of every class picks the shadow.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- explain the phases from the angle between the Sun, the Moon and Earth;
- say when a solar or lunar eclipse can happen, and why not every month;
- explain why there are two high tides a day.

## What Causes the Phases? {#phases}

One sentence carries this whole section: **the Moon is always half lit.** The
Moon makes no light of its own. The Sun lights the half facing it, all the
time. The phase you see is how much of that lit half happens to face Earth,
and that depends only on the angle between the Sun, the Moon and Earth.

You can see it with a lamp and a ball. A bare lamp in a dark room is the Sun.
A ball held at arm's length is the Moon. Your head is Earth. Turn slowly in a
circle and watch the ball:

- Ball toward the lamp: you see its dark side. **New moon.**
- A quarter of the way around: half the face is lit. **First quarter.**
- Ball opposite the lamp: the whole lit face points at you. **Full moon.**
- Three quarters of the way around: the other half lit. **Third quarter.**

In between come the crescents (less than half lit) and the gibbous phases
(more than half lit). While the lit part grows the Moon is **waxing**; while it
shrinks, **waning**. The full cycle, new moon to new moon, takes about 29.5
days.

Now the test for the shadow idea. Earth's shadow points straight away from the
Sun, so a shadow could only fall on a Moon opposite the Sun in the sky. But a
thin crescent Moon appears low in the west just after sunset, right next to
where the Sun went down. The shadow cannot explain it. In the lamp-and-ball
model, your head's shadow never touches the ball, except when the ball is
exactly behind your head. That is a lunar eclipse, and it is the only time
Earth's shadow plays any part.

Because the phase is an angle, it also tells time. A full moon is opposite the
Sun, so it rises at sunset. A first quarter Moon rises around noon and is
highest at sunset, which is why you often see the Moon in the afternoon.

## Why Not Every Month? {#eclipses}

A **solar eclipse** happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, so
only at new moon. A **lunar eclipse** happens when the Moon passes into Earth's
shadow, so only at full moon.

There is a new moon and a full moon every month. So why not an eclipse every
month? Because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit.
Picture two hula hoops tilted against each other. They cross at two points,
the **nodes**. Most months the new moon passes a little above or below the
Sun, and the full moon a little above or below Earth's shadow. An eclipse
needs a new or full moon right at a node. That lineup comes around about twice
a year, in what are called eclipse seasons.

Never look at the Sun, eclipse or no eclipse, without a proper solar filter.
Sunglasses are not a solar filter.

## Two Bulges, Two Tides {#tides}

The Moon's gravity gets weaker with distance. It pulls the ocean on the near
side of Earth more than it pulls Earth's center, and Earth's center more than
the ocean on the far side. That difference stretches Earth and its oceans into
two bulges, one facing the Moon and one facing away. Think of three runners on
one rope, pulled from the front: the group stretches at both ends.

Earth turns under both bulges every day, so most coasts get two high tides,
about every 12 hours and 25 minutes. The Sun raises tides too, a bit under half
as strong. At new and full moon the Sun and Moon line up and their tides add:
**spring tides**, the biggest range. At the quarter phases they work at right
angles: **neap tides**, the smallest.

::: {.callout-note title="Dr. Morgan's note"}
Do not memorize a phase chart. Learn to draw the top-down view, Sun on one
side, Earth in the middle, Moon at eight positions. From that one drawing you
can rebuild every phase, every rising time and both kinds of eclipse in about
thirty seconds. I have watched students do it on the exam.
:::

## Self-check

```{=html}
<div class="quiz" data-answer="d">
  <div class="question">1. The Moon is full tonight. Where is it at sunrise?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> High in the south</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> Rising in the east</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> Next to the Sun</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> Setting in the west</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>d</strong>. A full moon is opposite the Sun, so it rises as the Sun sets and sets as the Sun rises.
  </div>
</div>

<div class="quiz" data-answer="a">
  <div class="question">2. During a solar eclipse, what phase is the Moon in?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> New</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> First quarter</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> Full</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> Any phase, if the orbit lines up</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>a</strong>. The Moon must be between the Sun and Earth, which is new moon. A lunar eclipse needs a full moon.
  </div>
</div>
```

## Where this fits

The same habit, working out what you see from where things sit relative to
the Sun, explains the seasons in the next chapter. If you want to play with
the phases, the explorable for this lecture lets you move the Moon yourself.
